Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating perma-nent impairment of the visual system as it affects an individual’s ability to perform vision-related Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). The visual sys-tem includes the eyes and supporting structures, the neural pathways, and the visual cortex of the brain. Changes to the visual cortex are also discussed in Chapter 13, The Central and Peripheral Nervous System. For vision loss, that chapter follows the calculations presented here.

In accordance with the mandates of Chapters 1 and 2 of the Guides and with the principles of the International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities, and Handicaps (ICIDH)1 and the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF),2 this chapter focuses on vision, that is, on the functional impairment of the visual system as a whole. That system is unique in that it combines the input from 2 sepa-rate eyes into a single visual perception. The cal-culations in this chapter therefore do not consider anatomic changes to any component of the visual system by themselves, but only their functional consequences. For instance: they do not consider

the disfiguring aspect that may accompany an eye injury (see Section 11.3a and Table 11-5), nor do they consider the loss of vision in 1 eye without considering the remaining vision in the other eye (see Section 12.4b). The impairment ratings in this chapter estimate the severity of the effects of vision loss on the ability to perform vision-related ADLs. As explained in Chapters 1 and 2 (see Section 2.1), the assessment of impairment is only a first step toward disability assessment and deter-mination of monetary compensation; the ratings therefore do not consider the effect on specific job-related functions or on employability. Those aspects involve many factors that are beyond the scope of the Guides. One should remember that there are totally blind individuals who are gain-fully employed; there also are fully sighted indi-viduals who are unemployed.

In the Fifth Edition of the Guides this chapter was significantly revised from earlier editions. The revision was based on a consensus within the international community of experts in low vision. The visual acuity and visual field ranges on which the ratings are based were introduced in the 1970s and 1980s in the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision (ICD-9; 1977),3 the ICD-9 Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM; 1978),4 and ICIDH (1980),1 and were later confirmed in ICD-10 (1994)3 and in reports for the International Society for Low Vision Research and Rehabilitation (1999),5 the International Council of Ophthalmology (2002),6 and the World Health Organization (WHO; 2003)7. The Functional Vision Score (FVS) has been shown to correlate well with measures of Quality of Life.8–10 Additional background information is provided in companion publications to the Guides.11,12

Some important aspects of the differences between the current system and the system used in the Fourth Edition and earlier editions are:

1. The FVS, used now, estimates the ability to perform vision-related ADLs. The Visual Efficiency Scale (VES), used through the Fourth Edition, was based on employability estimates in 1925.13–16 That vision-specific scale predated by several decades the development of the Guides, but through various revisions had developed internal inconsistencies and was no longer based on current measurement standards. Like the VES, the FVS is an ability scale on which 0 indicates “no ability” and 100 indicates “normal ability.” The impairment rating for the visual system is calculated as: 100 − FVS.

Since the FVS scale is different from the earlier VES scale, visual impairment ratings based on the Fourth or earlier editions cannot be compared directly to impairment ratings based on the current edition.

2. The FVS is based primarily on an assessment of visual acuity and visual field, yet allows individ-ual adjustments for other functional deficits, such as contrast and glare sensitivity, color vision, bin-ocularity, stereopsis, suppression, and diplopia if these deficits cause a significant ability loss that is not reflected in the rating of the visual acuity or visual field loss. The previous system allowed corrections only for diplopia and aphakia; these separate scales are no longer needed.

3. Near-vision measurements, which are often inaccurate and were often omitted, are now optional; Section 12.5 contains a discussion on how to make the assessment of reading acuity more accurate.

12.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter of the Guides, the user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and with the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods for performing and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impair-ment evaluation.

Ophthalmology is able to precisely measure organ functions such as visual acuity and visual field. Therefore, this chapter uses visual acuity and visual field as the key factors (see Section 1.8c) on which the impairment evaluation is based. The resulting impairment ratings are statistical estimates of the ability loss that may result from a given impairment. Individual performance of certain tasks may be better or worse than the statistical average and may be further influenced by rehabilitative measures. The use of a statistical average is justified, because we do not want to disadvantage those who have made good adaptations by reducing their impairment rating. The case of Helen Keller may be quoted as an example of someone who made extraordinary adaptations despite very severe limitations. These adaptations should not have reduced her impairment rating.

The approach to impairment ratings in this chapter differs from that advocated in Section 1.8c, in which an impairment range (class) is determined first, based mainly on history and physical findings (see Table 1-5), and a percentage rating is assigned later. In this chapter, calculations based on visual acuity and visual field yield a percentage rating, from which the class or range follows. The number of ranges in this chapter (see Table 12-1 and following tables) is 1 more than in Table 1-3. This is because the Functional Vision Score can also be used for vision rehabilitation, where differentiation between severe and profound loss is needed and where combining all losses from 50% to 95% into 1 group is not meaningful. The internationally accepted FVS ranges are more similar to the detailed ranges of the Karnofsky Performance Status Scale17 than to the simplified ICF scale. The FVS ratings have been validated in several studies.8–10

The steps in calculating the FVS, and the visual system impairment rating (VSI) are summarized in Table 12-1.

Table 12-1 explains the steps involved in going from the measurements of visual functions (which indicate how the eyes function) to an estimate of functional vision (which indicates how the person functions).

12.1a Elements of a Visual Impairment Evaluation

Preparing an impairment evaluation report must be considered similar to providing expert testimony (see

Section 2.7). Section 12.6 contains a template that lists essential elements of any report. These include:

Current Visual Symptoms

List the current symptoms and complaints. Consider whether they explain the claimed ability loss.

Pertinent Visual History

Consider whether the history is consistent with the current complaints. Include:

• Causes of the current vision loss and other factors that may affect the individual’s ability to perform vision-related ADLs.

• Preexisting conditions and treatments and reasons for apportionment, if applicable (see Section 2.5c).

• Essential tasks of the job or occupation and how the visual deficits may affect these.

Pertinent Eye Exam

Consider whether the current findings are consistent with the current complaints. Consider whether Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI) has been reached. Include:

• Documentation of the current condition of the eyes and visual system and relevant anatomic findings.

• Visual acuity measurements with best correction, as detailed in Section 12.2.

• Visual field measurements for each eye, as detailed in Section 12.3.

An opinion about the ability to work and other employment-related factors may be requested. If sufficient information is available, such opinions may be given. However, such assessments are beyond the scope of the Guides (see Section 2.3b).

Note that although for diagnostic purposes the acuity of each eye separately is most important, for disability evaluation the acuity with both eyes open is most important. Accurate measure-ment of distance visual acuity (letter chart acuity) is mandatory; measurement of near acuity (reading acuity) is optional.

Visual Fields

Formal visual field studies are indicated, unless the patient waives any consideration of field loss. Use Section 12.3 to determine the Visual Field Score (VFS) (see Table 12-5) for the right eye and for the left eye; combine the plots to determine the binocular field and calculate the Functional Field Score (FFS) for the person (see Table 12-6). Note that although for diagnostic purposes the field of each eye separately is most important, for disability evaluation the binocular field is most important.

Functional Vision Score

Combine the Functional Acuity Score (FAS) and Functional Field Score (FFS) to derive the Functional Vision Score (FVS) as indicated in Section 12.4a. Note that the FVS is an ability score (0 = no ability, 100 = normal ability), whereas the

American Medical Association (AMA) impairment ratings rate loss (0 = no loss, 100 = total loss).

Visual System Impairment Rating

Calculate the Visual System Impairment (VSI) as 100 − FVS. If, applicable, include an adjustment for visual factors that are not reflected in the acuity or field score (see Section 12.4b).

Whole Person Impairment Rating

Calculate the whole person impairment rating (WPI) as indicated in Section 12.4c. If, applicable, combine this rating with unrelated nonvisual impairment ratings, using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix.

In addition to the equipment needed for a standard ophthalmologic evaluation, the following tools are required for the functional evaluation.

• Standardized letter chart. Use of a projector chart is acceptable for visual acuities of 20/100 or better. However, a lighted chart in a lighted room is preferred because it is more representative of normal viewing conditions. Charts with 5 letters per line, proportional spacing, and a logarithmic (geometric) progression of letter sizes are preferred.18–23 For vision in the normal and near-normal ranges, testing at 6 m (20 ft) is recommended. For testing in the low-vision range, testing at 1 m is recommended (see Table 12-2).24 Test charts for this distance are commercially available.25

• Standardized reading tests. Reading tests are optional. If performed, they should be standard-ized tests with continuous text segments as speci-fied in Section 12.5. A logarithmic progression of letter sizes is preferred. Letter size designations should be in M-units18 because the implementation of point size and Jaeger numbers has been shown to be inconsistent from chart to chart.

• Visual field equipment. If a restriction of the visual field is claimed or suspected, formal visual field testing on standardized equipment is required. Such tests often are performed by a technician, rather than by the examiner. If no visual field restriction is claimed, a confrontation visual field is acceptable to confirm the absence of field restrictions.

• Other functional tests, such as a contrast sensitivity test or glare test, if problems in these areas are reported.

• Samples of actual job-related tasks, if these tasks are different from average reading tasks.

12.1b Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Subjective symptoms of vision loss usually are the result of objective changes in visual acuity and/or visual field.

Visual acuity describes the ability of the eye to perceive details. Visual acuity loss will manifest itself in an inability to perform detail-oriented tasks, such as reading and face recognition. A lay term for visual acuity loss is blurred vision. Visual acuity loss affects many ADLs. Although visual acuity is gov-erned by only a small area of the retina (the fovea, the central-most area), it occupies a major part of the visual cortex.

Visual field refers to the ability to detect objects in the periphery of the visual environment. A lay term for peripheral field loss is tunnel vision. Visual field loss will manifest itself in an inability to detect peripheral objects and, often, in a reduced ability to avoid obstacles. The peripheral visual field occupies the largest part of the retina, but it occupies a smaller part of the visual cortex.

Good visual acuity and good visual field are both needed for the performance of daily living skills. A person with tunnel vision may not notice when someone enters the room. A person with visual acu-ity loss, on the other hand, may notice the newcomer but may have difficulty recognizing the person’s face. Once a person detects an object in peripheral vision, that person will use central vision to recog-nize it. A person with a visual field defect (tunnel vision) may not notice a sign on the road or on a wall but could read the sign once found, assuming the individual had good visual acuity. A person with normal visual fields but a visual acuity loss will detect the sign but will not be able to read it.

Another important function is contrast sensitivity. Whereas visual acuity is generally measured with small objects of high contrast, contrast sensitivity refers to the ability to detect larger objects of poor contrast. This ability is often needed for daily liv-ing skills. Facial characteristics are an example of typical low-contrast objects. Contrast sensitivity loss often accompanies visual acuity loss, but it can occur separately. Because measurement methods for contrast sensitivity are not standardized, this func-tion is not included in the impairment ratings. Where indicated, contrast sensitivity loss that exceeds the effects of the visual acuity loss (see Section 12.4b) may be handled as an individual adjustment.

Other symptoms may result from deficits in glare sensitivity, color vision, night vision, binocularity, stereopsis, suppression, and diplopia. If these deficits

cause a significant ability loss that is not reflected in a visual acuity or a visual field loss, they may also be handled as adjustments to the impairment rating (Section 12.4b).

12.1c Vision Rehabilitation

This book is mainly concerned with the assessment of impairments. However, it is the moral and profes-sional obligation of the medical professional to also point to rehabilitation as a way to offset the disabling effects of the impairment with enabling countermea-sures (see Section 1.3c). It is important to note that rehabilitation will not change the impairment or the impairment rating; it will only reduce the effect on participation.26

Successful vision rehabilitation needs to address many aspects of the problem:

Vision enhancement that will enable better use of the remaining vision. Vision enhancement aids include high plus reading glasses, magnifiers, illumination, and filters, etc.

Vision substitution will enable activities and partic-ipation by the subject through the use of aids based on other senses, such as Braille, long cane, talking books, etc.

Personal factors, such as depression and coping skills, need to be addressed. Providing appropriate vision rehabilitation may do more to lift a reactive depression than any medication may do.

The human environment, including family, school, or workplace and social groups, needs to be consid-ered. Supportive attitudes can be strongly enabling; prejudicial attitudes are disabling.

The physical environment can be similarly dis-abling through the erection of barriers or can be enabling by providing facilitators, such as workplace modifications, as mandated by the Americans with Disabilities Act.

These services require the efforts of a variety of rehabilitation specialists; they cannot be provided by the medical professional alone. However, it is the obligation of the medical profession to mention the existence of enabling options and to make the appro-priate referrals.

12.2 Impairment of Visual Acuity

12.2a Visual Acuity Notations

Visual acuity is usually recorded as a fraction com-paring the individual’s performance to a performance

standard. If the individual needs letters that are twice as large or twice as close as those needed by a stan-dard eye (ie, 2 × angular magnification), the visual acuity is 1/2. If letters are needed that are 5 times larger or 5 times closer, the visual acuity is 1/5, and so forth. In the United States, it is customary to standard-ize the numerator at 20. Thus, a visual acuity of 1/2 is recorded as 20/40 and a acuity of 1/5 is recorded as 20/100. Note that “normal” or “average” vision is better than the 20/20 reference standard. Thus, it is inappropriate to terminate visual acuity measurement at the 20/20 line or to refer to “20/20” as “normal vision,” let alone as “perfect vision.”27

12.2b Test Procedures

Visual acuity is usually measured with symbols (letters, numbers, pictures, or other symbols) presented in a letter chart format. It should be measured with best correction for the right eye (OD), for the left eye (OS) and with both eyes open (OU). Because the required letter sizes can vary widely, the optimum testing distance is not the same for all groups, as explained in the following paragraphs.

Testing in the Normal Range

Individuals in the normal and near-normal range of vision (20/60 or better, ICD-9-CM; see Table 12-2), represent the majority of all patients.4 The traditional letter charts and projector charts were designed for this group. The most common testing distance is 6 m (20 ft) because at this distance accommodation is relaxed and the optical difference with infin-ity may be ignored. When a printed chart is used, the indicated visual acuity values are valid only if the individual is located at the distance for which the chart was designed. If a projector chart is used, the individual must be located at the distance for which the projector was adjusted. Charts with a logarithmic progression of letter sizes, 5 letters on each row, and letter spacing that is equal to the letter size (often referred to as ETDRS-type charts, referring to the Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study) are the preferred standard.21,22 The original ETDRS pro-tocol (developed for research studies) uses 3 charts, 1 each for right, left, and both eyes. For disability assessment, the use of 1 chart for all 3 measurements is acceptable.

The individual is placed at the distance for which the chart was designed and encouraged to read as far down as possible. A line is considered read when the patient correctly reads more than half of the characters (eg, 3 of 5). Most charts will indicate the visual acuity value that corresponds to the ability to read each line. When visual acuity is measured in this way, the result should be recorded using the

standard US notation (ie, 20/…). The individual should be tested with the best available refractive correction. If an ETDRS-type chart is used, the VAS increases with 1 point for every letter the patient reads correctly.

When testing for visual acuities around the 20/200 level (“legal blindness”), the choice of letter chart is particularly important because it affects the assign-ment of benefits. On traditional charts that have no lines between 20/100 and 20/200, the descriptor “20/200 or less” becomes, effectively, “less than 20/100,” so individuals with 20/125 would be recorded as 20/200. On newer charts, which also have lines at 20/125 and 20/160, “20/200 or less” is more appro-priately interpreted as “less than 20/160” (see Table 12-2). If only an older printed chart is available, the individual can be brought to 10 ft so that “less than 20/160” can be interpreted as “less than 10/80.” The individual with 20/125 (10/63) is then reported appro-priately as better than 20/200. Note that the term legal blindness is a misnomer because 90% of individuals who have 20/200 or less visual acuity are not blind but have significant residual vision that can be enhanced through vision rehabilitation. The term severe vision loss, as used in ICD-9-CM, should replace the term legal blindness.**

Testing in the Low-Vision Range

Use of the Guides will often involve individuals whose visual acuity has dropped to less than 20/60 (ie, to the low-vision range in ICD-9-CM,4 (see Table 12-2). Individuals in the low-vision range form a minority of the general population but may represent the majority of those for whom visual impairment evaluations are requested.

Traditional letter charts often have only a few letters for visual acuities worse than 20/100. Such charts are inadequate for the low-vision range and have promoted the use of vague statements such as “count fingers” (CF) and “hand motions” (HM). More accurate results can be obtained by bringing the chart closer. Testing at 1 m is recommended because it can cover the entire low-vision range, down to 1/50 (20/1000).24

** Unfortunately, the Social Security Administration (SSA) in a ruling effective in 2007 has chosen to interpret “Statutory Blindness” in the context of Title II and Title XVI different from the usual definition of “legal blindness” in other federal, state and local laws and regulations. In the context of Title II and Title XVI, the SSA now interprets “20/200 or less” as “less than 20/100”, with the stipulation that even a single letter seen on a 20/100 line will disqualify the applicant.

When visual acuity is measured at 1 m, it should be recorded as a metric Snellen fraction, in which the numerator records the test distance in meters (in this case 1 m, thus 1/…) and the denominator indicates the smallest letter size read in “M-units” (1 M = 1.45 mm = about 1/16 in). The standard US notation may be added in parentheses. Thus, the ability to read 8 M characters at 1 m should be recorded as 1/8 (20/160). Charts with a cord attached to maintain the proper distance and labeled for 1-m testing are available commercially.25

Correction for Refractive Error

The visual acuity without correction may be reported as part of the general eye examination. The impair-ment ratings, however, should be based on the best-corrected visual acuity. It is important, therefore, to ensure that the refractive correction is appropriate for the testing distance. This is especially true for the short viewing distances used for patients with low vision. If uncorrected and best-corrected visual acuity are the same, this should be stated explicitly.

Monocular vs Binocular Acuity

Because binocular viewing (both eyes open) represents the most common viewing condition in daily life, the impairment rating should consider the best-corrected binocular visual acuity as well as the best-corrected acuity for each eye separately. Although the visual acuity of each eye is important for diagnostic considerations, for disability considerations the binocular value caries the larger weight.

Under most circumstances, best-corrected visual acuity measured binocularly will be determined by the acuity of the better eye. There are exceptions, however. People with latent nystagmus may have better eye stability, and hence better acuity, when viewing binocularly than when 1 eye is occluded. Some people with diplopia or with distortions in 1 eye may see better when the poorer eye is occluded.

Incomplete Data

Whenever possible, determination of an impairment rating should be based on direct examination of the individual. Occasionally, it may be necessary to deter-mine a tentative impairment rating based on chart review, when complete data may not be available. If no better information is obtainable, use the following:

Interpret CF ... — ft as .../200.

Interpret CF ... — m as .../60.

Interpret HM ... — ft as .../1000.

Interpret HM ... — m as .../300.

Therefore, CF 3 ft is interpreted as 3/200 (VAS = 10), and HM 5 ft is interpreted as 5/1000 (VAS = 1). Tests of finger counting and of hand movements at shorter distances also assess the central field and therefore should not be considered as proper visual acuity measurements.

If the best-corrected visual acuity with both eyes open is not available and cannot be obtained, it may be assumed that vision with both eyes open is equal to the best-corrected acuity of the better eye.

Use of Realistic Conditions

The evaluation of visual functions should be based on performance under optimal conditions. An excep-tion can be made, however, when the best possible conditions are not feasible in daily life. Examples include individuals who would see better with con-tact lenses but who cannot tolerate them; those with a large interocular difference in refractive error who cannot tolerate full correction of both eyes; and those who can achieve better acuity with an extremely high or extremely low illumination level that cannot be achieved under normal daily living conditions or in the workplace.

Under these and similar conditions, the evaluation should be based on measurements obtained under realistic daily living (or working) conditions. Document why testing under suboptimal conditions is most appropriate. When testing multiply disabled individuals, a distinction must be made between failure to see and failure to respond.

The 3 parts of Table 12-2 fit well with each other. This confirms that the VAS is a reasonable esti-mate of acuity-related visual abilities and that the impairment rating is a reasonable estimate of acuity-related performance loss. This has been confirmed in several studies.8–10 The right side of Table 12-2 may be used to obtain an impression of the effect of various impairment levels. Additional examples may be found in Table 12-4. Also note that these ranges closely resemble the ICF ranges in Table 1-3; the main difference is that the ICF ranges combine severe and profound loss into 1 broad range.

It should be remembered that the dividing lines between the ranges do not indicate stepwise increases in ability. They are like mileposts along a road. They provide useful reference points, but the landscape does not change suddenly when a marker is passed; rather, the landscape changes gradually and continuously between the markers.

2. Combine the visual acuity scores (VAS) to obtain a functional acuity score (FAS) for the person.

After the best-corrected visual acuity values for binocular vision (OU), for the right eye (OD), and for the left eye (OS) have been obtained and converted to Visual Acuity Scores, these values need to be combined to a single Functional Acuity Score (FAS) for the person to provide an estimate of that person’s ability to perform acuity-related daily living tasks. This is done using Table 12-3.

The formula for combining the Visual Acuity Scores (VAS) for OU, OD, and OS (see Table 12-3) is:

FAS = (3 × VASOU + VASOD + VASOS)/5

In this calculation the binocular acuity provides 60% of the weight; the right and left eye each contribute 20%.

Note that the person’s FAS is not simply the VAS of the better eye. For example, an individual with 1 blind eye will have a 0 VAS for that eye. If the other eye is normal, the FAS will be near-normal, but not as good as when both eyes were normal. See the legend for Table 12-4.

The acuity-related impairment rating is calculated by subtracting the FAS from 100. Note that the FAS can be larger than 100 but that the impairment rating is truncated at 0.

12.3 Impairment of the Visual Field

12.3a Test Procedures

If no visual field impairment is claimed (by the patient) or suspected (by the physician), a confronta-tion visual field may be used to confirm a normal field (visual field impairment rating = 0). In all other circumstances (visual field impairment rating >0), formal visual field tests should be performed by qualified personnel according to the instructions provided with the equipment.

Confrontation Visual Field

This method uses only the examiner’s hands. Seated in front of the individual, the examiner moves his or her hands from the periphery inward to test for the peripheral field limits. This method is an acceptable way to confirm a normal visual field in individuals in whom no field loss is claimed, but it is too gross for a proper evaluation in cases where a field loss is claimed or suspected.

Tangent Screen Testing

This method uses a flat, black screen on which vari-ously sized objects may be moved. This method is difficult to standardize and loses accuracy beyond 45°. It is not acceptable for the accurate assessment of permanent impairment.

Goldmann-Type Testing

The Goldmann visual field equipment provided the first standardized field measurement technique. Testing is done in a bowl so that all testing distances are equal while the background and stimulus luminances can be controlled tightly. The usual mode of testing is known as kinetic perimetry because an operator moves a test stimulus of constant size and intensity.

The test results are plotted as isopters, contour lines that outline the areas where stimuli of various intensi-ties can be perceived. The functional implications of certain isopter patterns are relatively easy to interpret. Agencies, such as the Social Security Administration, often require testing of the Goldmann III-4-e isopter for eligibility determinations.

Automated Perimetry

In recent decades, there has been a move from manual to automated perimetry. (Commonly used equip-ment includes Humphrey, Octopus, Dicon, and other brands.) This has been accompanied by a move to static perimetry. In static perimetry, the stimulus is not moved; the presentations are limited to various fixed locations where stimulus size and intensity are varied.

Automated perimetry results are commonly plotted as a gray scale. Such reports are better suited for automated statistical analysis. They are less intuitive for human interpretation with regard to functional vision. Most clinical tests are limited to the central 30° radius because this is the most important area for medical diagnostic purposes. For the functional assessment of visual field loss, however, testing to a 60° radius or beyond is mandatory.

Binocular Fields

Considering both monocular and binocular function is even more important for a functional assessment of the field of vision than it is for visual acuity because intact field areas in one eye may compensate for field loss in the other eye. In cases of asymmetric field loss, the binocular field of view may be substantially better than the field of either eye alone.

Direct testing of the binocular visual field presents problems, however, because the amount of conver-gence in a bowl perimeter cannot be monitored and fixation monitoring devices will not work when the head, rather than the eye, is centered. Therefore, the

fields of each eye should be measured separately, and a binocular field plot should be derived from the superimposition of the two monocular field plots.

Tests Used

When Goldmann equipment is used, the III-4-e isopter should be plotted. If only a larger isopter is available, this isopter may be used, but it should be understood that this may result in an underestima-tion of the field loss (FFS too high). If only smaller isopters are available, the test cannot be used for impairment evaluation, since this would result in an overestimation of the field loss (FFS too low). One study has shown that using the V-4-e isopter instead of the III-4-e one increases the FFS (decreases the impairment rating) by about 20 ponts.29

When automated, static perimetry is used, the results are displayed as a gray scale, not as isopters. Therefore, a pseudoisopter equivalent to the Goldmann III-4-e isopter must be constructed as explained in Example 12-8 and Fig 12-5A and 12-5B. On the Humphrey equipment, this would be the isopter for a 10-dB stimulus. Plots of the central 30° are the plots most often used for medical diagnostic purposes. If these are the only plots available, the assumption must be made that the field beyond 30° is completely normal, which may result in an underestimation of the actual field loss; therefore, seeking a full-field Humphrey plot or a Goldmann plot is advisable. Only if the remaining field radius on the 30° central plot is smaller than 20° in all directions and confrontation testing indicates no further peripheral vision or remaining temporal islands (as may happen in retinitis pigmentosa [RP]), the combination of a central Humphrey plot and a peripheral confrontation test may be used.

12.3b The Visual Field Score

The VFS, which is the basis for the calculation of visual field–based impairment ratings, parallels the VAS. The VAS can be determined by counting the letters read correctly on a standardized visual acuity chart. Similarly, the VFS can be determined by counting the points seen on a standardized visual field grid. The combination rules are also similar.

Testing Grid

The testing grid is constructed by drawing 10 meridians: 2 in each of the upper quadrants and 3 in each of the lower quadrants. The optimal positions for the 10 meridians are as follows: 25°, 65° (upper right), 115°, 155° (upper left), 195°, 225°, 255° (lower left), 285°, 315°, and 345° (lower right). Along these meridians, 5 points (spaced 2° apart) are assigned to the central 10° and 5 points (spaced 10° apart) are assigned to the periphery beyond 10°; thus, a

60° radius will represent 10 points. The nasal and superior meridians may not reach 60°, but the lateral field will extend further. Thus, the average normal field will score about 100 points.

Figure 12-1 summarizes the point assignments. The circle represents a 10° radius.

This arrangement has the following effects:

• The Visual Field score (VFS) for the central 10° is 50 points. This reflects the fact that the central 10° area of the visual field corresponds to 50% of the primary visual cortex.

• This choice maintains the traditional assumption that a visual field loss to a 10° radius is equally disabling as a visual acuity loss to 20/200.

• Functionally, it also means that 50 points are assigned to the central field, which is important for reading and manual activities, and 50 points are assigned to the peripheral field, which is important for mobility.

• Choosing the measured meridians within the quadrants rather than along the horizontal and vertical meridians avoids the need for special rules for hemianopias.

• A complete homonymous hemianopia receives a 50-point score. This implies that it is considered equally disabling as a field restriction to a 10° radius or as a visual acuity loss to 20/200.

• Choosing 3 meridians in the lower quadrants and 2 in the upper quadrants acknowledges the functional importance of the lower field by giving it 50% extra weight.

• ICD-9-CM defines severe, profound, and near-total visual field loss as concentric restriction to a 10°, 5°, and 2.5° field radius.4 These categories fit the VFS scale.

12.3e Calculating the Binocular Field

Existing perimeters are not equipped to provide reliable measurements of the binocular visual field.

Therefore, the binocular visual field is constructed by superimposing the two monocular plots. On the superimposed plot, only areas missed by both eyes are counted as defects; areas seen by either one of the eyes are counted as seen. The resulting binocular score can vary dramatically, depending on the loca-tion of the defects.

Therefore, the FAS and the FFS are combined using a multiplication formula, as is used to combine other unrelated impairments.

Basic Rule

To calculate the FVS, the FAS and the FFS are mul-tiplied as if they represented percentage scores:

FVS = (FAS × FFS)/100

For example, if the FAS is 80 (a 20% impairment) and the FFS is 75 (a 25% impairment), the FVS is calculated as follows: 80% × 75% = 60% (a 40% impairment).

Note that this calculation can be performed only on the basis of the residual ability scores. Any calcula-tions (adding, averaging, or multiplying) based on the impairment ratings (which indicate ability loss) would give erroneous answers. The combined effect of two impairment ratings is not easily captured in a simple formula but can be derived from the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix which also shows that 20% impairment + 25% impairment → 40% impairment.

Additional Rules

Some additional rules are needed to avoid unrealistic calculations.

1. For the purpose of this calculation, Functional Acuity and Functional Field Scores that are greater than 100 are treated as if they were 100. Thus, losses are counted only if the performance drops below the performance standard. The average performance of healthy eyes often is better than the performance standard (20/20). This better performance is taken into account in calculating the Functional Acuity or Field Scores (see Example 12-2), but it is not counted as a reduction of the impairment rating.

2. If visual field data are not available and if the patient agrees that there is no clinical reason to suspect visual field loss, the FFS may be assumed to be 100. In this case, the FVS is the same as the FAS, and the impairment rating for the visual system is the same as the impairment rating for the visual acuity loss.

Rule for Central Scotomata, Where Field Loss and Acuity Loss Are Not Independent

The dense array of points in the central 10° area of the visual field grid means that paracentral scoto-mata (blind spots adjacent to the point of fixation) will be counted even if they do not affect the central acuity. This is appropriate because it has been shown that such scotomata can interfere significantly with reading ability and with other ADLs.

However, if the scotoma is central (ie, it covers the point of fixation), it affects both visual acuity and visual field and the 2 impairment ratings can no longer be treated as independent. Using the basic formula, central scotomata would be counted twice: once through their effect on visual acuity and once through their effect on the central field. Therefore, a third additional rule is needed.

3. If visual acuity is reduced, some central visual field losses will not be counted, as specified in Table 12-9.

Thus, for every 10 points of VAS loss, field losses in one ring of 10 grid points are ignored. This means that these points are counted as if they were seen. This adjustment is made for each eye separately. The effect of this rule is that individuals with a small island of good acuity within a pericentral scotoma (blind spot surrounding the point of fixation) will get credit for this scotoma, but that those with a central scotoma that affects visual acuity will not get double benefits. The adjustment does not affect peripheral field losses. Thus, a person with periph-eral field loss due to glaucoma who also has a central loss due to macular degeneration will get credit for the central loss as well as for the peripheral field loss (see Examples 12-15 through 12-17).

12.4b Individual Adjustments

Although visual acuity loss and visual field loss represent significant aspects of visual impairment, they are not the only factors that can lead to a loss of functional vision and to a limitation in the ability to perform ADLs. This edition of the Guides does not provide detailed scales for other functions, such as the following:

• Contrast sensitivity. This is the ability to perceive larger objects of poor contrast. Loss of this abil-ity can interfere significantly with many ADLs. It is often, but not always, associated with a loss of visual acuity.

• Glare sensitivity (veiling glare), delayed glare recovery, photophobia (light sensitivity), and reduced or delayed light and dark adaptation. These are other functions that may interfere with proper contrast perception.

• Color vision defects. These defects are not uncom-mon but usually do not interfere significantly with generic ADLs. Severe color vision defects (achromatopsia) are usually accompanied by visual acuity loss. In some vocational settings the impact of minor color vision deficiencies can be significant. This is one example of the fact that generic impairment ratings may not reflect job-specific employability ratings. As has been stated earlier (see Sections 12.1a, 2.4b), assessment of the employment-related consequences of vision loss is important but is beyond the scope of these Guides.

• Binocularity, stereopsis, suppression, and diplo-pia. These functions vary in their effect on ADLs. Their significance often depends on the environ-ment and vocational demands.

Standardized measurement techniques on which standardized ability estimates can be based have not yet been developed for most of these functions. Furthermore, their effect may be partially accounted for by a loss of visual acuity and may vary signifi-cantly according to environmental demands.

If significant factors remain that affect functional vision and that are not accounted for through visual acuity or visual field loss, a further adjustment of the impairment rating of the visual system may be in order. The need for the adjustment must be well documented. The adjustment should be limited to an increase in the impairment rating of the visual sys-tem (reduction of the FVS) by, at most, 15 points.

The following benchmarks may be used to judge the effect of additional impairments on the ability to perform ADLs.

A 5-point loss can result from a 5-line acuity loss in one eye (20/20 + 20/60), since (3 × 100 + 100 + 75)/5 = 95. It can also result from a 1-line acuity loss in both eyes (20/25 + 20/25), since (3 × 95 + 95 +

95) /5 = 95.

A 10-point loss can result from a 10-line acuity loss in one eye (20/20 + 20/200), since (3 × 100 + 100 + 50)/5 = 90. It can also result from a 2-line acuity loss in both eyes (20/30 + 20/30), since (3 × 90 + 90 + 90)/5 = 90.

A 20-point loss can result from the total loss of one eye (20/20 + NLP), since (3 × 100 + 100 + 0)/5 =

80. It can also result from a 4-line acuity loss in both eyes (20/50 + 20/50), since (3 × 80 + 80 + 80)/5 =

80. Note that the equivalence of 20/50 in both eyes to total loss of one eye has been unchanged since 1925. Additional impairments will be less severe than total loss of one eye, hence the limitation to 15 points.

These examples also demonstrate why the AMA Guides do not allow visual impairment ratings that do not consider binocular vision since a rat-ing of only one eye does not provide an accurate assessment of the overall functioning of the person. Although it is mathematically possible to calculate a rating for one eye, this calculation would not be realistic, since the outcome of that calculation would only equal the AMA impairment rating for the per-son if both eyes were affected to the same extent.*

The same rule should be observed as in the case of central scotomata. Deficits should only be counted to the extent that their effect exceeds the effect of the related visual acuity or visual field deficit. Note the following examples.

1. An individual with a congenital dark adaptation deficit with normal acuity and normal visual fields may be given a limited impairment rating based on this deficit. In someone with rod dystrophy (as in RP) manifested by field loss as well as dark adaptation problems, the impairment rating will be determined by the field loss and no additional rating is given for the dark adaptation deficit.

2. Many people with visual acuity loss due to macular degeneration also have a loss of contrast sensitivity. Because the impairment rating is dominated by the visual acuity loss, no additional

3. Congenital red-green color vision deficits exist in about 7% of males, acquired color vision deficits also exist. These deficits do not interfere with generic ADLs and do not receive an impairment rating. A printer with such a deficit would have no problems with black-and-white printing, but he or she may have difficulty judging the accuracy of color prints. This deficit does not enter into the functional impairment considerations in this chapter (see Figure 12-1 and Sections 2.1) since it affects employability in a specific job. Total color blindness (achromatopsia) is extremely rare. It is accompanied by visual acuity loss, in which case the visual acuity loss will determine the impairment rating.

4. Diplopia may exist in varying degrees. Not only the angle and the existence of diplopia should be considered but also the extent to which it interferes with ADLs and the extent to which suppression may reduce the awareness of double vision. In the rare event that the diplopia is so severe that it warrants continuous occlusion of one eye, that eye may be counted as having no vision (see Section 12.2b), which results in a 20 point loss (see the list earlier in this section). By comparison, continuous occlusion of 1 full quadrant of gaze might be counted as a 5-point reduction. For other conditions, the examiner should use reasonable judgment.

12.4c Impairment of the Whole Person

Individuals with mild, moderate, and severe vision loss (classes 1, 2, and 3a) may benefit from vision enhancement techniques such as large print, opti-cal or electronic magnification, better illumination, and better contrast. In classes beyond this range, a shift to vision substitution techniques occurs; this may include talking books, Braille, and long cane. Because of these techniques, a totally blind person is not totally incapacitated. In the previous section, a downward adjustment of the FVS of up to 15 points was allowed for additional impairments whose effect exceeds that of the visual acuity and/or visual field loss. A similar, but opposite, adjustment is made in classes 3a, 3b, and 4 to account for the effects of vision substitution skills that alleviate the effects of the permanent vision loss.

This adjustment affects the translation of the impair-ment rating of the visual system (VSI) to an impair-ment rating of the whole person (WPI) as shown in Table 12-8. Since the effectiveness of vision substitution skills will vary from person to person and cannot be predicted from the visual acuity and visual field measurements, the adjustments in Table 12-8 are generalized estimates. That the WPI is not reduced further, even for blind persons who have made very effective adjustments, reflects the fact that vision substitution skills alleviate the effects of vision loss but do not eliminate the vision loss itself.

The rule is as follows:

If the VSI is <50%, WPI = VSI. If the VSI is >50%, WPI = 50 + 0.7 × (VSI − 50)

Figure 12-8 illustrates this graphically.

At this point it may also be appropriate to consider apportionment between preexisting conditions and the effect of the current injury (see Sections 12.1a and 2.5c).

12.4d Nonvisual Impairments

Nonvisual impairments are not rated as part of the visual system. If a visual condition is accompanied by facial disfigurement, this is rated according to Table 11-5. The resulting impairment rating (if any) is then combined with the visual impairment rating of the whole person, using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix. It should be remembered that the effects of facial disfigurement are often job related. While facial disfigurement may have mini-mal consequences for a telephone operator, it would be significant for a receptionist who greets people. Assessment of job-related effects is beyond the scope of these Guides (see Section 2.1). The same holds true for other nonvisual impairments.

12.5 Visual Acuity Measurement at Near (Reading Acuity)

Consideration of reading acuity in the calculation of the Functional Acuity Score (FAS) is optional. It is warranted only if the reading acuity is significantly dif-ferent from the distance acuity. In that case, it is appro-priate to use the average of the FAS for letter chart acuity, as discussed earlier, and the FAS for reading, as shown in Table 12-11. This section contains instructions for accurate reading acuity measurement.

12.5a Near Acuity vs Distance Acuity (Reading Acuity vs Letter Chart Acuity)

Near acuity may be measured with a reduced-size letter chart or with continuous text. When the objec-tive is the assessment of functional vision—as is the purpose of these Guides—continuous textual read-ing material should be used.

Under most circumstances, letter chart acuity and reading acuity—if measured appropriately and with the proper refractive correction—will be similar. If significant differences between reading acuity and letter chart acuity exist, measurement errors, inappro-priate refractive correction, and/or other complicating factors should first be suspected. The nature of these factors needs to be explored, documented, and cor-rected where possible. Accurate calculation of the reading acuity requires accurate measurement of the letter size (see Section 12.5b) as well as of the view-ing distance. Many practitioners record only the letter size that has been read and not the reading distance. Table 12-11 shows that this is inappropriate because small changes in the reading distance can result in significant changes in visual acuity, especially if the reading distance is short. For this reason, the magnification requirement for read-ing acuity may be somewhat greater than that for letter acuity. The difference is known as the magnification reserve needed for reading fluency.

12.5b Letter Size Notations

Another reason for discrepancies can be found in the use of inaccurate letter size notations. The com-monly used Jaeger numbers refer to the labels on the boxes in the printing house in Vienna where Jaeger selected his print samples in 1854. They have no numerical value, and their implementation on current reading cards is notoriously variable. The J-numbers listed in Table 12-11 present the range of J-designa-tions found for each letter size when 20 current read-ing cards were surveyed. All current letter sizes were larger than Jaeger’s original ones. Note that a range of 4 Jaeger sizes is not uncommon.

Some charts use a notation in printer’s points. Point sizes have a numerical value but may vary depending on the type style used (eg, 8-pt Arial = 9-pt Times Roman). Many reading cards list distance equiva-lents. This notation is valid only if the card is used at the distance for which the card was designed. At any other distance, the use of distance equivalents is utterly confusing.

The only letter size unit that is based on a well-defined standard and thus allows a comparison between letter chart acuity and reading acuity is the M-unit. M-units are based on Snellen’s original definition and refer directly to the actual letter size (X-height for uppercase letters on a letter chart, x-height for lowercase letters in a reading segment). In either case, 1 M-unit subtends 5 minutes of arc at 1 m and equals 1.454 mm (10% less than 1/16 inch).

12.5c Measurement Guidelines for Reading Acuity (Near-Vision Acuity)

Visual acuity measurement at near is more complex than visual acuity measurement at distance because both letter size and viewing distance can vary. When reading acuity is measured, follow these guidelines.

If binocular reading is possible, the binocular reading acuity should be recorded. If binocular reading is not possible or not preferred, the reading acuity of the eye that is preferred for actual reading should be used.

The measurement of reading acuity requires a read-ing card with calibrated reading segments. Cards with proportionally spaced segments of equal length are

preferred. The preferred step size is the same as for let-ter charts. The viewing distance should be measured and recorded carefully. Measurement with a diopter ruler simplifies calculations (see Section 12.5d) and provides a direct comparison to the required accommo-dation or reading add. Letter size specification in M-units is mandatory if any calculations or comparisons are involved. One M-unit equals 1.454 mm, which is slightly smaller than 1/16 in. Measuring the letter size in units of 1/16 in overestimates the visual acuity by slightly less than half a standard step size.

To test reading acuity for the normal and near- normal range, many cards are available. Most will indicate distance equivalents. Note that these distance equivalents are valid only if the designated distance is used. Reading cards with a cord attached for the correct reading distance are recommended.25

Many individuals undergoing impairment evaluation will fall in the low-vision range. They may require shorter reading distances and/or larger print sizes. Table 12-11 shows the proper visual acuity values and impairment ratings for many combinations of letter size and viewing distance.

12.5d Modified Snellen Formula

The visual acuity values found in Table 12-11 could be calculated using the standard form of the Snellen fraction V = m/M, in which the viewing distance is specified in meters (1 m = 100 cm = 40 in; 1 in = 2.5 cm) and the letter size in M-units. Use of the standard Snellen fraction becomes awkward when the viewing distance (in meters) is itself a fraction. In this case, it is more convenient to use the recipro-cal of the viewing distance, which is known as the diopter (2 D = 1/2 m, 5 D = 1/5 m, etc). The use of reciprocal values also has the advantage of turning the Snellen fraction into a multiplication, which is more easily calculated in one’s head because it uses whole numbers instead of fractions within fractions.

The traditional formula

V = m/M

thus becomes

1/V = M/m = M × 1/m = M × D

where M = letter size in M-units, m = viewing dis-tance in meters, and D = viewing distance in diopters.

12.5e Instructions

To find the optimal combination of reading distance and letter size, start at the reading distance that cor-responds to the individual’s current reading add and/or accommodative power. Increase the reading add

(reduce the reading distance) to reach smaller print. Using Table 12-11, find the visual acuity at the inter-section of the letter size row and the reading distance column. Alternatively, using the M × D formula and a diopter ruler, calculate the 1/V value. For each combi-nation of viewing distance and letter size read, compare the reading add to the viewing distance in diopters to verify the appropriate refractive correction. Also, com-pare the M × D value to verify that the visual acuity values are consistent.

12.5f Correction of Refractive Error

To verify that the refractive correction is appropriate for the viewing distance, it is often useful to ask the

individual to move the card back and forth to find the best possible focus. If the refractive correction (reading add) is not optimal for the distance used, the measured acuity will not be the best-corrected visual acuity. Measurement of the reading distance in diopters has the advantage of easy comparison to the reading addition.

Overlays for Conversion of Goldmann Visual Field Plots

General

The Goldmann plot shows isopters. These are lines that outline the area where a particular stimulus can be seen. The AMA visual field impairment rating is based on the area where the III4e stimulus can be seen.

The area where the stimulus can be seen depends on the size and brightness of the stimulus. A larger stimulus will be seen in a larger area. For diagnostic purposes it is common to plot several isopters. For the AMA calculations, only the III4e isopter is rel-evant; any additional isopters should be ignored.

If only smaller isopters have been plotted, the AMA rating cannot be calculated, since it would be pos-sible to increase the field loss to any desired degree by reducing the stimulus.

If only a larger isopter (IV4e or V4e) has been plot-ted, the result will be an underestimation of the field loss compared to the III4e isopter. The difference may vary from person to person and is not insignificant. In one study an average difference of 20 VFS points was found between the III4e and V4e isopters.29

Copy a Goldman Visual Field Plot to sheets of ace-tate as used for overhead projectors. Do this twice.

1. Place one transparency over the Goldmann plot for the Right eye.

2. Using a dry-erase or similar marker, mark the points outside the III4e isopter with a forward slash (/). If there are blind spots within this isop-ter, also mark the points inside the blind spot.

The number of points that were seen (not marked)

determines the Visual Field Score (VFS) for the Right eye. This number is easily calculated by considering that there are 50 small dots and 50 closed dots. If any of the open dots (beyond 600) were seen, they are added to the VFS.

Calculate the number of points seen for the bin-ocular field.

Overlays for Conversion of Humphrey visual field plots

General

Humphrey visual field plots do not describe an isop-ter as do Goldmann fields. They describe the sensi-tivity at various points of a grid, but the Humphrey grid is different from the AMA grid.

The points on the AMA grid used to calculate the Visual Field Score (VFS) are dense in the center and sparser in the periphery, to reflect differences in the functional significance of various visual field areas; the VFS score is based on points seen. The points on the Humphrey (HFA) grids are evenly spaced, to detect diagnostically significant structural losses. Therefore, a one-to-one correlation of the two grids is impossible. In the center one HFA point may cor-respond to several VFS points; in the periphery sev-eral HFA points contribute to one VFS point.

The HFA 10-2 plot corresponds to the inner 50 VFS points.

The HFA 30-2 and 24-2 plots cover 20 of the outer 50 VFS points and provide an estimate of the inner 50 VFS points. If a 10-2 plot is available (preferable), only the 20 outer points are counted from these grids. If a 10-2 plot is not available, the central 16 HFA points are used to estimate the central 50 VFS points.

The HFA 60-4 plot covers the outermost 30 of the VFS points.

Instructions

Copy the diagrams (Figure 12-11) on page 317 to a sheet of acetate as used for overhead projectors. Cut the sheet to separate the diagrams for the right and the left eye.

1. Place the appropriate diagram over each HFA plot of absolute threshold values. Each number of the HFA plot should appear in the center of one of the small squares.

Each circle in the conversion diagrams cor-responds to one VFS point. If the circle is in a square that corresponds to one HFA number, it is counted as seen (HFA >10) or not seen (HFA <10)

based on that HFA number. If the circle is in an area containing more than one HFA number, it is counted based on the average HFA value.

2. Using a dry-erase or similar marker, mark each of the small circles where the threshold sensitivity is above 10. If the circle is in an area that covers more then one number, mark it if the average is above 10. On the diagonals, some HFA numbers straddle a line; count them for both areas.

If a central VFS cell contains a number, that cell

is counted multiple times to arrive at the VFS score. For instance: if the cell contains “4x” the value of that one HFA number determines the seen or missed status of four VFS points.

3. For each diagram, count the unmarked circles. This corresponds to the VFS points that were not seen. For each eye: add the not-seen counts for the 60-4 and 30-2 fields and for the 10-2 field, if available. This constitutes the not-seen count for each eye.

Note that points can only be claimed as missed if

they have been tested. If a 60-4 plot is not avail-able the outer points cannot be claimed as lost; this limits the claimant’s field loss score. Have a 60-4 test or a Goldmann test done to prevent this.

4. To determine the binocular field, superimpose the plots for the right and the left eye and count the points that have not been marked in either eye. This is the count of points missed in binocular vision.

5. Calculate the weighted average of points missed to obtain the Visual Field Impairment rating. (OD + OS + 3x OU) / 5 =

Subtract this number from 100 to obtain the

Functional Field Score (FFS) for the person.

6. Make a photocopy of the diagrams for documen-tation. If a dry-erase marker was used, wipe the acetate clean to be used for another subject.
